summary.title: Authorization in a microservices world
summary.one_liner: Learn how to move from a simple admin flag to RBAC and ABAC in microservices, using a policy enforcement point, policy decision point and policy information point, with a Node.js example.
keywords: how do i add authorization to microservices
takeaways: Authorization evolves from a boolean admin flag to roles (RBAC) and then attribute-based rules (ABAC) as business logic grows.
Use the PEP/PDP/PIP/PAP model: a middleware enforces decisions, a policy engine decides, and an information point loads the application data policies need.
Avoid direct database reads across service boundaries; options are attaching data to calls, syncing copies, or a separate data service.
Per-service authorization middleware and libraries are presented as a good balance; RBAC can be done by matching route paths and HTTP verbs.
A Node.js/Express example defines policies alongside routes and uses JSON path expressions to reference request and user data in conditions.
summary.summary: The author recounts a monolithic PHP app where authorization checks lived inside controllers, then explains why this becomes hard to maintain. He describes a general authorization flow built from PEP, PDP, PIP and an optional PAP, and compares three microservice architectures: a central authorization service, an authorization service plus a data service, and per-service middleware and libraries. The final sections show RBAC as route-and-verb matching and an Express.js example in which policies are declared with routes and conditions reference loaded data via JSON paths.
